formulas.title: Correlated Multivariate Uncertainty Propagation
formulas.description: Computes the first-order propagated variance $\sigma_f^2$ of a smooth function $f(x_1,\dots,x_m)$ of correlated measured variables $x_i$ from its partial derivatives $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}$ and the input covariance matrix $\mathrm{Cov}(x_i, x_j)$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Linear error propagation maps the local covariance ellipsoid of experimental input variables through the Jacobian of a derived physical observable.
formulas.intuitive_summary: The squared uncertainty of a calculated quantity combines how sensitive the formula is to each input with both the individual uncertainties and how pairs of inputs fluctuate together.
formulas.interpretation: Diagonal terms ($i = j$) recover standard quadrature addition of independent uncertainties, whereas off-diagonal covariance terms ($i \ne j$) can either increase or partially cancel the net variance depending on the relative signs of the sensitivities and correlations.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the bilinearity of statistical covariance applied to the first-order multivariate Taylor expansion $\delta f \approx \sum_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\delta x_i$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Accurate when input uncertainties are small relative to the curvature scale of $f$; strongly nonlinear functions or asymmetric distributions require second-order Hessian terms or Monte Carlo propagation.

\\sigma_f^2.name: Propagated Variance
\\sigma_f^2.description: Variance of the derived observable $f$ induced by fluctuations in the measured inputs.

f.name: Derived Observable Function
f.description: Differentiable physical function mapping measured inputs $x_i$ to a target quantity.

x_j.name: Paired Input Variable
x_j.description: The $j$-th experimentally measured input quantity paired with $x_i$ in the covariance sum.

\\mathrm{Cov}(x_i, x_j).name: Input Covariance Matrix Element
\\mathrm{Cov}(x_i, x_j).description: Statistical covariance $\mathbb{E}[(x_i - \mu_i)(x_j - \mu_j)]$ quantifying joint fluctuations between $x_i$ and $x_j$.

formulas.title: Weighted Least-Squares Chi-Squared Statistic
formulas.description: Defines the dimensionless weighted least-squares objective $\chi^2(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ as the sum of squared residuals between $N$ independent measurements $y_i$ and model predictions $f(x_i; \boldsymbol{\theta})$, each normalized by its measurement standard deviation $\sigma_i$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The chi-squared objective weights every data point inversely by its variance so precise measurements exert stronger pull on fitted physical parameters than noisy measurements.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Measures the total mismatch between data and model in units of each measurement's error bar, squaring and summing the deviations across all points.
formulas.interpretation: Minimizing $\chi^2(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ yields the minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator (Gauss-Markov theorem) for linear models and coincides with maximum likelihood estimation under independent Gaussian noise.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Arises directly from the negative twice log-likelihood of $N$ independent normal random variables with means $f(x_i; \boldsymbol{\theta})$ and variances $\sigma_i^2$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Assumes independent, normally distributed residuals with accurately known variances $\sigma_i^2$ and negligible uncertainty in the independent coordinates $x_i$.

\\chi^2(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).name: Chi-Squared Statistic
\\chi^2(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).description: Dimensionless sum of variance-weighted squared residuals evaluated at parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.name: Model Parameter Vector
\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.description: Vector of $p$ unknown physical parameters adjusted during model fitting.

N.name: Number of Data Points
N.description: Total number of independent experimental observations in the dataset.

y_i.name: Observed Data Value
y_i.description: Measured value of the dependent observable at index $i$.

f(x_i; \\boldsymbol{\\theta}).name: Model Prediction
f(x_i; \\boldsymbol{\\theta}).description: Theoretical prediction evaluated at independent coordinate $x_i$ and parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

\\sigma_i.name: Measurement Standard Deviation
\\sigma_i.description: Known one-sigma Gaussian uncertainty associated with observation $y_i$.

formulas.title: Reduced Chi-Squared Goodness-of-Fit
formulas.description: Normalizes the minimized chi-squared statistic $\chi^2$ by the number of statistical degrees of freedom $\nu = N - p$, where $N$ is the number of data points and $p$ is the number of freely fitted model parameters.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Reduced chi-squared provides a scale-free diagnostic of whether observed residuals are consistent with the assumed measurement uncertainties.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Divides the total squared error-bar mismatch by the number of independent constraints left after fitting the model; a good fit sits close to one.
formulas.interpretation:
For a correctly specified linear model with accurate Gaussian uncertainties, $\mathbb{E}[\chi^2_
u] = 1$ with standard deviation $\sqrt{2/
u}$; $\chi^2_
u \gg 1$ indicates model inadequacy or underestimated errors, while $\chi^2_
u \ll 1$ suggests overestimated errors or overfitting.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the expectation value $\mathbb{E}[\chi^2] = \nu$ of a Pearson chi-squared random variable with $\nu = N - p$ independent standard normal degrees of freedom.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Strictly exact for linear models with independent Gaussian errors and $N > p$; in nonlinear models or constrained fits, the effective number of degrees of freedom can deviate from $N - p$.

\\chi^2_\\nu.name: Reduced Chi-Squared
\\chi^2_\\nu.description: Chi-squared statistic per degree of freedom.

\\chi^2.name: Minimized Chi-Squared Statistic
\\chi^2.description: Value of the weighted sum of squared residuals at the best-fit parameters.

N.name: Number of Observations
N.description: Total count of data points entering the fit.

p.name: Number of Fitted Parameters
p.description: Number of independent model parameters optimized against the data.

formulas.title: Generalized Correlated-Covariance Chi-Squared
formulas.description: Generalizes the chi-squared objective to correlated measurements by contracting the residual vector $\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{f}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with the inverse covariance matrix $\mathbf{C}^{-1}$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Measures the squared Mahalanobis distance between the data vector and theoretical prediction in the metric defined by the correlated experimental noise covariance.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Extends weighted least squares to datasets where errors are correlated across bins by weighting residuals with the inverse covariance matrix instead of individual variances.
formulas.interpretation: When $\mathbf{C}$ is diagonal ($C_{ij} = \sigma_i^2 \delta_{ij}$), the quadratic form collapses to standard weighted least squares; when off-diagonal correlations are present, $\mathbf{C}^{-1}$ down-weights redundant correlated modes and isolates independent combinations of measurements.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Invariant under invertible linear basis transformations of the data space, representing the exact exponent of the multivariate Gaussian likelihood.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Requires $\mathbf{C}$ to be symmetric positive definite and well-conditioned; empirical covariance matrices estimated from finite simulations require Hartlap or Bayesian debiasing corrections upon inversion.

\\chi^2(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).name: Generalized Chi-Squared Statistic
\\chi^2(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).description: Dimensionless Mahalanobis quadratic form quantifying correlated data-model discrepancy.

\\mathbf{y}.name: Measurement Data Vector
\\mathbf{y}.description: Column vector of $N$ correlated experimental observations.

\\mathbf{f}(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).name: Model Prediction Vector
\\mathbf{f}(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).description: Column vector of $N$ theoretical predictions parameterized by $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

\\mathbf{C}^{-1}.name: Inverse Covariance Matrix
\\mathbf{C}^{-1}.description: Precision matrix obtained by inverting the $N \times N$ data covariance matrix $\mathbf{C}$.

\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.name: Model Parameter Vector
\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.description: Vector of unknown model parameters being inferred.

formulas.title: Maximum Log-Likelihood Score Equation
formulas.description: Specifies the first-order stationarity condition for the maximum likelihood estimator by setting each component of the score vector $\frac{\partial \ln \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_k}$ to zero.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Selects the parameter vector that maximizes the probability density of the observed dataset under an arbitrary statistical noise model.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Finds the parameter values that make the actually observed experimental data most probable by locating the peak of the log-likelihood surface.
formulas.interpretation: Because the logarithm is strictly increasing, maximizing $\ln \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ converts products of independent observation probabilities into tractable sums while preserving the exact location of the maximum; for non-Gaussian Poisson or exponential data, it avoids the bias inherent in Gaussian chi-squared approximations.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Equivariant under smooth reparameterizations $\boldsymbol{\phi} = g(\boldsymbol{\theta})$: the maximum likelihood estimate of a transformed parameter is simply $g(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Requires $\ln \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ to be differentiable in the interior of parameter space; maxima occurring on physical boundaries or multimodal likelihoods must be checked via global optimization and negative-definite Hessian verification.

\\mathcal{L}(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).name: Likelihood Function
\\mathcal{L}(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).description: Joint probability or probability density of the observed data viewed as a function of parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.name: Parameter Vector
\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.description: Full vector of unknown model parameters.

\\theta_k.name: Parameter Component
\\theta_k.description: The $k$-th scalar component of the parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

formulas.title: Fisher Information Matrix Element
formulas.description: Defines the $(j,k)$ element of the Fisher information matrix $\mathcal{I}_{jk}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ as the negative expectation value of the second partial derivative (Hessian) of the log-likelihood $\ln \mathcal{L}$ with respect to parameters $\theta_j$ and $\theta_k$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Quantifies the average amount of statistical information an observable dataset carries about simultaneous variations in model parameters through the curvature of the log-likelihood peak.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Measures how sharply peaked the log-likelihood surface is on average: a steeper peak means larger Fisher information and tighter constraints on the parameters.
formulas.interpretation: Under standard regularity conditions, $\mathcal{I}_{jk}$ equals the covariance of the score vector $\mathbb{E}[(\partial_j \ln \mathcal{L})(\partial_k \ln \mathcal{L})]$, is symmetric positive semidefinite, and transforms as a covariant metric tensor on the statistical manifold; its inverse approximates the parameter covariance matrix.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Acts as the unique (up to scale) Riemannian metric on probability distributions invariant under sufficient-statistic Markov morphisms (Chentsov's theorem).
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Requires interchangeability of differentiation and integration over the data support; fails when the support of the distribution depends on $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ or when parameters are strictly degenerate ($\det \mathcal{I} = 0$).

\\mathcal{I}_{jk}(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).name: Fisher Information Matrix Element
\\mathcal{I}_{jk}(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).description: Expected curvature element measuring joint sensitivity of the log-likelihood to parameters $\theta_j$ and $\theta_k$.

\\ln \\mathcal{L}.name: Log-Likelihood
\\ln \\mathcal{L}.description: Natural logarithm of the likelihood function evaluated over the random data.

\\theta_j.name: Row Parameter
\\theta_j.description: The $j$-th parameter component differentiated in the log-likelihood Hessian.

\\theta_k.name: Column Parameter
\\theta_k.description: The $k$-th parameter component differentiated in the log-likelihood Hessian.

formulas.title: Cramér-Rao Variance Lower Bound
formulas.description: Establishes the fundamental lower bound on the variance $\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})$ of any unbiased estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of an unknown parameter $\theta$ as the reciprocal of the Fisher information $\mathcal{I}(\theta)$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Sets the ultimate statistical precision limit achievable by any unbiased data-analysis algorithm given a fixed experimental noise model.
formulas.intuitive_summary: No unbiased way of estimating a physical parameter from noisy data can ever achieve a smaller variance than one over the Fisher information.
formulas.interpretation: An unbiased estimator that achieves equality is called efficient and attains minimum variance; in the multivariate case, the covariance matrix $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) - \mathcal{I}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ is positive semidefinite, providing a benchmark for experimental design and optimal estimator construction.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Derived directly from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the covariance between the unbiased estimator $\hat{\theta}$ and the zero-mean score function $\partial_\theta \ln \mathcal{L}$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Applies strictly to unbiased estimators under standard Fisher regularity conditions; biased estimators (such as ridge or shrinkage estimators) can achieve lower variance at the expense of nonzero bias.

\\mathrm{Var}(\\hat{\\theta}).name: Estimator Variance
\\mathrm{Var}(\\hat{\\theta}).description: Mean squared statistical scatter $\mathbb{E}[(\hat{\theta} - \theta)^2]$ of the unbiased estimator $\hat{\theta}$.

\\hat{\\theta}.name: Unbiased Parameter Estimator
\\hat{\\theta}.description: Function of the observed data satisfying $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta}] = \theta$.

\\mathcal{I}(\\theta).name: Scalar Fisher Information
\\mathcal{I}(\\theta).description: Expected negative second derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to $\theta$.

\\theta.name: True Physical Parameter
\\theta.description: Underlying unknown scalar parameter being estimated from experimental observations.

formulas.title: Bayes Posterior Probability Theorem
formulas.equation: P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid D, M) = \frac{P(D \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, M)\,P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid M)}{P(D \mid M)}
formulas.description: Relates the posterior probability density $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid D, M)$ of model parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ given experimental data $D$ and hypothesis $M$ to the product of the likelihood $P(D \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, M)$ and prior density $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid M)$, normalized by the marginal likelihood $P(D \mid M)$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Bayes's theorem is the fundamental rule of consistent probabilistic inference, updating prior knowledge about physical parameters in light of newly observed experimental data.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Your updated belief about a parameter after taking data is proportional to how plausible that parameter was beforehand multiplied by how well it explains the observed measurement.
formulas.interpretation: For parameter estimation within a fixed model $M$, the denominator $P(D \mid M)$ is independent of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and acts purely as a normalization constant, whereas for comparing competing models it becomes the decisive Bayesian evidence.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows directly from the product rule of conditional probability, $P(A, B) = P(A \mid B)P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A)$, and is uniquely selected as the variational minimizer of Kullback-Leibler divergence under data constraints.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Applies universally whenever a well-defined forward likelihood $P(D \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, M)$ and proper (or locally integrable) prior $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid M)$ exist; in the large-sample Bernstein-von Mises limit, the posterior concentrates around the maximum-likelihood estimator independently of smooth non-vanishing priors.

P(\\boldsymbol{\\theta} \\mid D, M).name: Posterior Probability Density
P(\\boldsymbol{\\theta} \\mid D, M).description: Updated probability density over parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ conditioned on observed data $D$ and model $M$.

\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.name: Parameter Vector
\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.description: Vector of unknown physical or instrumental parameters inferred from measurement.

D.name: Observed Experimental Data
D.description: Realized dataset or measurement record collected by the detector.

M.name: Physical Model Hypothesis
M.description: Assumed theoretical framework specifying the forward generative relation between $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and $D$.

P(D \\mid \\boldsymbol{\\theta}, M).name: Likelihood Function
P(D \\mid \\boldsymbol{\\theta}, M).description: Sampling probability density of observing data $D$ for fixed parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ under model $M$.

P(\\boldsymbol{\\theta} \\mid M).name: Prior Probability Density
P(\\boldsymbol{\\theta} \\mid M).description: Probability density encoding pre-data physical constraints and background information on $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

P(D \\mid M).name: Marginal Likelihood (Bayesian Evidence)
P(D \\mid M).description: Normalization constant equal to the prior-averaged likelihood of the observed data under model $M$.

formulas.title: Marginal Likelihood (Bayesian Evidence)
formulas.equation: Z = P(D \mid M) = \int P(D \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, M)\,P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid M)\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}
formulas.description: Defines the Bayesian evidence $Z = P(D \mid M)$ as the integral of the likelihood $P(D \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, M)$ weighted by the prior density $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid M)$ over the full parameter space $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The marginal likelihood quantifies the overall probability of generating the observed dataset under model $M$ averaged across all a priori plausible parameter configurations.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Instead of judging a theory only by its single best-fitting parameter point, the evidence averages how well the theory predicts the data across its entire allowed parameter volume, penalizing wasted complexity.
formulas.interpretation: Mathematically isomorphic to the canonical partition function in statistical physics, $Z$ rewards high peak likelihood while automatically penalizing excessive prior volume through an intrinsic Occam factor.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the sum rule of probability and unit normalization $\int P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid D, M)\,d\boldsymbol{\theta} = 1$ applied to Bayes's posterior theorem.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Requires a strictly proper normalized prior $P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid M)$ to remain finite and well-calibrated; improper flat priors leave $Z$ undefined up to an arbitrary multiplicative constant.

Z.name: Bayesian Evidence
Z.description: Shorthand notation for the marginal likelihood $P(D \mid M)$ of model $M$, analogous to a statistical-mechanical partition function.

P(D \\mid M).name: Marginal Likelihood
P(D \\mid M).description: Prior-averaged probability density of observing dataset $D$ under hypothesis $M$.

P(D \\mid \\boldsymbol{\\theta}, M).name: Likelihood Function
P(D \\mid \\boldsymbol{\\theta}, M).description: Probability density of data $D$ conditioned on specific parameter values $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

P(\\boldsymbol{\\theta} \\mid M).name: Prior Probability Density
P(\\boldsymbol{\\theta} \\mid M).description: Normalized prior probability density over the parameter manifold of model $M$.

\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.name: Parameter Vector
\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.description: Multi-dimensional integration variable spanning all free parameters of model $M$.

formulas.title: Bayes Factor for Model Comparison
formulas.description: Defines the Bayes factor $B_{12}$ as the ratio of the marginal likelihoods (Bayesian evidences) $P(D \mid M_1)$ and $P(D \mid M_2)$ of two rival physical models $M_1$ and $M_2$ evaluated on the same dataset $D$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Bayes factor measures the exact strength of experimental evidence favoring hypothesis $M_1$ over $M_2$, converting prior model odds into posterior model odds.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A Bayes factor greater than one means the data are more probable overall under model 1 than under model 2, automatically balancing goodness of fit against model simplicity.
formulas.interpretation: By Bayes's theorem at the model level, posterior odds satisfy $P(M_1 \mid D)/P(M_2 \mid D) = B_{12}\,P(M_1)/P(M_2)$; values $\ln B_{12} > 5$ correspond to decisive evidence on the empirical Jeffreys scale.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Arises from dividing the model-level posterior probabilities of $M_1$ and $M_2$, canceling the universal data normalization $P(D)$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid for both nested and non-nested physical hypotheses, provided both models use proper normalized priors on any non-shared parameters and are evaluated on the exact same dataset $D$.

B_{12}.name: Bayes Factor
B_{12}.description: Dimensionless evidence ratio quantifying relative data support for model $M_1$ versus model $M_2$.

P(D \\mid M_1).name: Evidence of Model 1
P(D \\mid M_1).description: Marginal likelihood of observed dataset $D$ under the first competing hypothesis $M_1$.

P(D \\mid M_2).name: Evidence of Model 2
P(D \\mid M_2).description: Marginal likelihood of observed dataset $D$ under the second competing hypothesis $M_2$.

D.name: Observed Experimental Data
D.description: Common measurement dataset used to compare both hypotheses.

formulas.title: Jeffreys Reparameterization-Invariant Prior
formulas.description: Constructs the non-informative Jeffreys prior density $P_J(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ proportional to the square root of the determinant of the Fisher information matrix $\mathcal{I}_{ij}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\mathbb{E}[\partial_i \partial_j \ln P(D \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})]$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Jeffreys's rule defines a canonical objective prior volume element on a statistical manifold that yields identical posterior inferences under arbitrary smooth reparameterizations.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Places more prior weight where the measurement apparatus is most sensitive to parameter changes, ensuring that changing units or coordinates never alters your physical conclusions.
formulas.interpretation: In information geometry, $\mathcal{I}_{ij}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ is the Riemannian metric tensor induced by the local quadratic expansion of Kullback-Leibler divergence, so $\sqrt{\det \mathcal{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is the invariant Riemannian volume form.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from diffeomorphism covariance under smooth coordinate transformations $\boldsymbol{\phi} = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$, under which $\mathcal{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = J^T \mathcal{I}(\boldsymbol{\phi}) J$ and $\sqrt{\det \mathcal{I}}$ transforms identically to a probability density.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Produces a uniform prior for location parameters and a scale-invariant $1/\sigma$ prior for scale parameters; in high-dimensional multi-parameter models, reference priors may be preferred to avoid marginalization paradoxes.

P_J(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).name: Jeffreys Invariant Prior Density
P_J(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).description: Coordinate-invariant objective prior probability density over parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

\\mathcal{I}(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).name: Fisher Information Matrix
\\mathcal{I}(\\boldsymbol{\\theta}).description: Expected negative Hessian matrix of the log-likelihood measuring local parameter distinguishability.

\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.name: Parameter Vector
\\boldsymbol{\\theta}.description: Coordinate vector on the statistical parameter manifold.

formulas.title: Nuisance-Parameter Posterior Marginalization
formulas.description: Obtains the marginalized posterior probability density $P(\theta_1 \mid D)$ for a physical parameter of interest $\theta_1$ by integrating the full joint posterior $P(\theta_1, \boldsymbol{\eta} \mid D)$ over all nuisance parameters $\boldsymbol{\eta}$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Marginalization rigorously eliminates unwanted calibration, background, and systematic parameters while propagating their full uncertainty and covariance into the inferred physical quantity.
formulas.intuitive_summary: To find the true uncertainty on one physical parameter, you average the posterior over every plausible value of all the messy calibration and background parameters rather than freezing them at a guess.
formulas.interpretation: When posterior samples are drawn via Markov chain Monte Carlo, marginalization over $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ is achieved effortlessly by projecting the sampled chain onto the $\theta_1$ coordinate and discarding the nuisance columns.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows directly from the continuous sum rule of probability theory applied to the joint posterior distribution.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Requires integrable nuisance priors; strong nonlinear degeneracies between $\theta_1$ and $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ can widen or skew the marginalized posterior relative to conditional slices at fixed $\boldsymbol{\eta}$.

P(\\theta_1 \\mid D).name: Marginalized Posterior Density
P(\\theta_1 \\mid D).description: Posterior probability density of the target physical parameter $\theta_1$ after integrating out nuisance variables.

\\theta_1.name: Parameter of Interest
\\theta_1.description: Primary physical quantity targeted for scientific inference.

\\boldsymbol{\\eta}.name: Nuisance Parameter Vector
\\boldsymbol{\\eta}.description: Vector of calibration, background, or auxiliary parameters required by the forward model but not of primary interest.

P(\\theta_1, \\boldsymbol{\\eta} \\mid D.name: Joint Posterior Density
P(\\theta_1, \\boldsymbol{\\eta} \\mid D.description: Full multi-dimensional posterior distribution over both target and nuisance parameters.

formulas.title: Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)
formulas.description: Approximates minus twice the log Bayesian evidence in the large-sample limit as $\mathrm{BIC} = k\ln N - 2\ln \hat{\mathcal{L}}$, balancing the maximized log-likelihood $\ln \hat{\mathcal{L}}$ against a complexity penalty proportional to the number of free parameters $k$ and the logarithm of the sample size $N$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Schwarz's Bayesian Information Criterion provides a rapid, prior-independent asymptotic proxy for Bayesian model comparison when full multi-dimensional evidence integration is impractical.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Rewards a model for fitting the data well through $-2\ln \hat{\mathcal{L}}$, but charges a tax of $\ln N$ for every extra free parameter it introduces; the model with the lowest BIC wins.
formulas.interpretation: In the asymptotic limit $N \to \infty$, the Bayes factor between two models satisfies $-2\ln B_{12} \approx \mathrm{BIC}_1 - \mathrm{BIC}_2$, making BIC asymptotically consistent for selecting the true data-generating model.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Obtained by taking $-2\ln Z$ of the Laplace saddle-point evidence approximation, substituting $\det \mathbf{H} \propto N^k$ for $N$ independent observations, and dropping $O(1)$ prior-dependent constants.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid only for regular, unimodal likelihoods in the large-sample regime $N \gg k$ with independent observations; fails when parameters hit physical boundaries, models are singular, or prior volume effects dominate.

\\mathrm{BIC}.name: Bayesian Information Criterion
\\mathrm{BIC}.description: Dimensionless asymptotic model-selection score; smaller values indicate stronger statistical support.

k.name: Number of Free Parameters
k.description: Dimensionality of the continuous parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ estimated from the data.

N.name: Sample Size
N.description: Number of independent experimental data points or observations.

\\hat{\\mathcal{L}}.name: Maximized Likelihood
\\hat{\\mathcal{L}}.description: Peak value of the likelihood function $P(D \mid \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, M)$ attained at the maximum-likelihood estimate.

formulas.title: Laplace Gaussian Approximation to Bayesian Evidence
formulas.description: Approximates the $k$-dimensional Bayesian evidence integral $Z$ around the posterior mode $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ as the product of the peak likelihood $\hat{\mathcal{L}}$, the prior density $P(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$, and the Gaussian covariance volume $(2\pi)^{k/2}(\det \mathbf{H})^{-1/2}$ determined by the negative log-posterior Hessian matrix $\mathbf{H}$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Laplace approximation applies multivariate saddle-point integration to evaluate the marginal likelihood analytically, explicitly separating goodness of fit from the Occam volume factor.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Approximates the posterior peak as a multi-dimensional bell curve so the evidence integral equals the peak height times the width of the bell curve relative to the prior.
formulas.interpretation: Factorizing $Z \approx \hat{\mathcal{L}} \times \left[P(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})(2\pi)^{k/2}(\det \mathbf{H})^{-1/2}\right]$ isolates the maximum likelihood from the dimensionless Occam factor, which measures the fraction of prior volume consistent with the data.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Derived directly from the second-order Taylor expansion of $\ln[P(D \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, M)P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid M)]$ at its stationary point $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ followed by exact multivariate Gaussian integration.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Accurate for sharply peaked, unimodal posteriors far from parameter-space boundaries in high signal-to-noise regimes; breaks down for multi-modal, strongly skewed, or heavy-tailed posteriors where nested sampling is required.

Z.name: Approximate Bayesian Evidence
Z.description: Saddle-point approximation to the marginal likelihood $P(D \mid M)$.

\\hat{\\mathcal{L}}.name: Peak Likelihood
\\hat{\\mathcal{L}}.description: Likelihood function evaluated at the posterior mode $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$.

P(\\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\theta}}).name: Prior Density at Mode
P(\\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\theta}}).description: Prior probability density evaluated at the posterior peak $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$.

k.name: Parameter Space Dimension
k.description: Number of continuous model parameters integrated over.

\\mathbf{H}.name: Negative Log-Posterior Hessian Matrix
\\mathbf{H}.description: Symmetric positive-definite $k \times k$ curvature matrix $H_{ij} = -\partial_i \partial_j \ln[P(D \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}, M)P(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid M)]|_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}$.

formulas.title: Wiener-Khinchin Power Spectral Density Theorem
formulas.description: Relates the power spectral density $S_x(\omega)$ of a wide-sense stationary stochastic process $x(t)$ to the continuous Fourier transform of its temporal autocorrelation function $R_{xx}(\tau) = \langle x(t)x(t+\tau)\rangle$ over lag time $\tau$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Wiener-Khinchin theorem establishes an exact duality between time-domain temporal correlations and frequency-domain variance distribution for stationary random processes.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A noisy signal that stays correlated over long times concentrates its variance at low frequencies, whereas a signal that forgets its past almost instantly spreads its power evenly across all frequencies.
formulas.interpretation: Because $R_{xx}(\tau)$ is real and even for real stationary processes, $S_x(\omega)$ is guaranteed to be real, even, and non-negative, and its integral over all frequencies $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} S_x(\omega)\,d\omega = R_{xx}(0)$ recovers total mean-squared signal power.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from time-translation invariance (wide-sense stationarity) combined with unitary Fourier harmonic decomposition.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Requires wide-sense stationarity and absolute integrability of $R_{xx}(\tau)$ (or distributional interpretation via Dirac delta lines for embedded periodic components); non-stationary processes require Wigner-Ville or short-time spectral representations.

S_x(\\omega).name: Power Spectral Density
S_x(\\omega).description: Mean-squared signal variance per unit angular frequency at $\omega$ (shown for a voltage observable $x$).

\\omega.name: Angular Frequency
\\omega.description: Harmonic angular frequency coordinate conjugate to lag time $\tau$.

R_{xx}(\\tau).name: Autocorrelation Function
R_{xx}(\\tau).description: Ensemble expectation $\langle x(t)x(t+\tau)\rangle$ measuring temporal correlation across lag $\tau$.

\\tau.name: Time Lag
\\tau.description: Temporal separation between two evaluations of the stationary process.

formulas.title: Nyquist-Shannon Critical Sampling Criterion
formulas.description: States the minimum uniform sampling frequency $f_s$ required to reconstruct a continuous band-limited signal containing no frequency components above $f_{\max}$ without spectral aliasing.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem defines the exact threshold between lossless digital discretization and irreversible high-frequency folding.
formulas.intuitive_summary: To capture a wave faithfully without confusing fast wiggles for slow ones, you must sample it at least twice per cycle of its fastest oscillation.
formulas.interpretation: Multiplying a continuous waveform by a Dirac impulse comb of spacing $1/f_s$ replicates its Fourier spectrum every $f_s$; the condition $f_s \ge 2 f_{\max}$ guarantees that adjacent spectral copies remain disjoint so an ideal low-pass sinc filter recovers the exact original waveform.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Arises from the Poisson summation formula and the discrete translation invariance of periodic sampling lattices in conjugate time-frequency domains.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Strictly applies to baseband signals band-limited to $|f| < f_{\max}$ sampled uniformly over infinite duration; real-world finite-duration acquisition requires guard bands, anti-aliasing filters, and windowing to suppress spectral leakage.

f_s.name: Sampling Frequency
f_s.description: Number of discrete analog-to-digital samples acquired per second.

f_{\\max}.name: Maximum Signal Frequency
f_{\\max}.description: Upper cutoff bandwidth of the band-limited continuous signal.

formulas.title: Schottky Discrete-Charge Shot Noise Spectrum
formulas.description: Gives the single-sided current noise power spectral density $S_I(f)$ arising from independent Poissonian arrivals of discrete charge carriers of charge $q$ carrying average direct current $I$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Schottky's shot noise formula quantifies the fundamental white-noise floor imposed by the quantization of electric charge or photon arrivals in non-equilibrium transport.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Because electric current consists of individual electrons rather than a smooth fluid, their random arrival times create a steady, frequency-independent hiss proportional to the average current.
formulas.interpretation: Integrating $S_I(f)$ over a measurement bandwidth $\Delta f$ yields mean-squared current fluctuations $\langle \delta I^2\rangle = 2 q I \Delta f$, establishing the standard quantum limit for photodetection and vacuum-tube or p-n junction current measurements.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the Wiener-Khinchin transform of a memoryless stationary Poisson impulse train with independent carrier transit events.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid for frequencies far below the inverse carrier transit time ($f \ll \tau_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}$) and uncorrelated Poissonian transport; Coulomb repulsion or Pauli exclusion in mesoscopic conductors suppresses noise below $2qI$ by a sub-Poissonian Fano factor $F < 1$.

S_I(f).name: Single-Sided Current Noise Spectral Density
S_I(f).description: Mean-squared current fluctuation per unit linear frequency bandwidth.

q.name: Elementary Charge
q.description: Magnitude of the discrete charge carried by each independent particle ($e \approx 1.602\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$).

I.name: Mean Electric Current
I.description: Time-averaged direct current flowing across the barrier or detector.

formulas.title: Hooge Empirical Flicker Noise Power Spectrum
formulas.description: Models low-frequency $1/f^\gamma$ flicker voltage noise spectral density $S_V(f)$ across a biased conductor with direct voltage $V$, total mobile carrier count $N_c$, empirical dimensionless Hooge parameter $\alpha_H$, and spectral exponent $\gamma \approx 1$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Hooge's relation captures the ubiquitous low-frequency pink-noise excess observed in solid-state electronics, arising from broad distributions of trapping and mobility fluctuation timescales.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Slowly fluctuating defects and carrier-mobility traps cause resistance noise that grows stronger at lower frequencies, scaling up with bias voltage and down as the device contains more carriers.
formulas.interpretation: Superposing independent Lorentzian two-level fluctuators over a wide log-uniform distribution of activation times generates $S_V(f) \propto 1/f$, which dominates over white thermal and shot noise below the $1/f$ corner frequency and motivates AC modulation techniques.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Reflects approximate scale invariance across decades of relaxation timescales in disordered condensed-matter ensembles.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Empirical scaling law valid over intermediate frequency decades ($0.8 \lesssim \gamma \lesssim 1.4$); strictly $1/f$ behavior must roll off at ultra-low and ultra-high frequencies to keep integrated noise power finite.

S_V(f).name: Voltage Noise Power Spectral Density
S_V(f).description: Mean-squared voltage fluctuation per unit linear frequency at frequency $f$.

\\alpha_H.name: Hooge Parameter
\\alpha_H.description: Dimensionless material- and quality-dependent constant characterizing bulk flicker noise strength (typically $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-2}$).

V.name: Applied Bias Voltage
V.description: Mean direct-current voltage drop across the conducting sample.

N_c.name: Total Number of Mobile Carriers
N_c.description: Total count of free charge carriers participating in conduction within the active volume.

f.name: Linear Frequency
f.description: Fourier frequency at which the flicker noise spectrum is evaluated.

\\gamma.name: Flicker Spectral Exponent
\\gamma.description: Dimensionless power-law slope near unity ($\gamma \approx 1$ for pure pink noise).

formulas.title: Matched-Filter Optimal Signal-to-Noise Ratio
formulas.description: Determines the maximum achievable squared signal-to-noise ratio $\rho_{\mathrm{opt}}^2$ when detecting a known deterministic waveform with Fourier transform $\tilde{h}(f)$ embedded in stationary additive Gaussian noise of single-sided power spectral density $S_n(f)$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The optimal matched-filter SNR defines the theoretical ceiling of linear coherent detection in colored stationary noise via noise-weighted inner products.
formulas.intuitive_summary: By dividing out the noise floor at every frequency before correlating with the expected signal template, a matched filter extracts every bit of signal energy from quiet frequency bands while automatically ignoring noisy bands.
formulas.interpretation: Derived from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on the noise-weighted inner product $(a|b) = 4\,\mathrm{Re}\int_0^\infty \frac{\tilde{a}^*(f)\tilde{b}(f)}{S_n(f)}\,df$, the equality is saturated exclusively by the whitened matched filter $\tilde{K}(f) \propto \tilde{h}(f)/S_n(f)$, central to radar and LIGO gravitational-wave detection.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from Parseval's inner-product isometry and Hilbert-space Cauchy-Schwarz optimality under the positive-definite metric $S_n^{-1}(f)$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Optimal for additive stationary Gaussian noise and an accurately known template $\tilde{h}(f)$; non-Gaussian glitches or waveform parameter mismatches degrade sensitivity and require veto chisquare tests and template banks.

\\rho_{\\mathrm{opt}}.name: Optimal Signal-to-Noise Ratio
\\rho_{\\mathrm{opt}}.description: Dimensionless ratio of peak matched-filter output amplitude to root-mean-square noise.

\\tilde{h}(f).name: Signal Fourier Transform
\\tilde{h}(f).description: Frequency-domain complex amplitude of the target waveform (unit shown for dimensionless strain $h(t)$).

S_n(f).name: Single-Sided Noise Power Spectral Density
S_n(f).description: Background instrumental noise variance per unit linear frequency (unit shown for dimensionless strain).

formulas.title: Lock-In Phase-Sensitive Demodulated Output
formulas.description: Gives the low-pass-filtered direct-current output voltage $V_{\mathrm{out}}$ of a phase-sensitive lock-in amplifier demodulating a sinusoidal input of amplitude $V_s$ against a unit-amplitude coherent reference shifted by phase offset $\Delta\phi$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Phase-sensitive demodulation translates a narrowband carrier signal down to DC while rejecting all out-of-band noise and incoherent interference outside the low-pass filter bandwidth.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Multiplying a modulated signal by a synchronized reference wave shifts the target signal to a steady DC voltage proportional to $\cos\Delta\phi$, while noise at other frequencies averages away to zero.
formulas.interpretation: Using the trigonometric product identity $\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}t + \phi_s)\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}t + \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}) = \frac{1}{2}\cos\Delta\phi + \frac{1}{2}\cos(2\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}t + \phi_s + \phi_{\mathrm{ref}})$, low-pass filtering removes the $2\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}$ harmonic; pairing with a $90^\circ$-shifted reference recovers the quadrature output $\frac{1}{2}V_s\sin\Delta\phi$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from harmonic orthogonality of sinusoidal basis functions over integer cycles under synchronous frequency mixing.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Assumes a pure sinusoidal reference (square-wave switching introduces odd-harmonic responses weighted by $1/n$) and a low-pass cutoff frequency well below $2 f_{\mathrm{ref}}$ so the sum-frequency ripple is fully attenuated.

V_{\\mathrm{out}}.name: Demodulated DC Output Voltage
V_{\\mathrm{out}}.description: Filtered in-phase direct-current voltage proportional to the synchronous signal component.

V_s.name: Modulated Signal Amplitude
V_s.description: Peak voltage amplitude of the incoming sinusoidal carrier signal.

\\Delta\\phi.name: Signal-Reference Phase Difference
\\Delta\\phi.description: Relative phase angle $\phi_s - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ between the input signal and internal reference oscillator.

formulas.title: Two-Sample Allan Variance Frequency Stability
formulas.description: Defines the two-sample Allan variance $\sigma_y^2(\tau)$ as half the mean-squared difference between adjacent non-overlapping fractional frequency averages $\bar{y}_k$ and $\bar{y}_{k+1}$ evaluated over averaging time $\tau$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Allan variance is the standard time-domain metrology diagnostic for oscillator and clock stability, remaining finite even in the presence of non-stationary flicker and random-walk frequency noise.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Instead of comparing every frequency measurement to a long-term average that may drift forever, the Allan variance compares each time slice only to its immediate neighbor, cleanly separating fast random noise from slow drift.
formulas.interpretation: In the frequency domain, $\sigma_y^2(\tau) = 2\int_0^\infty S_y(f)\frac{\sin^4(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f\tau)^2}\,df$; the $f^2$ transfer zero at DC regularizes $1/f$ and $1/f^2$ divergences so log-log slopes of $\sigma_y(\tau)$ uniquely identify white, flicker, and random-walk noise regimes.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Constructed from first-order discrete time differencing of consecutive boxcar averages, yielding a translation-invariant two-sample estimator with zero sensitivity to constant frequency offsets.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Converges for power-law frequency noise $S_y(f) \propto f^\alpha$ with $\alpha \ge -2$ (down to random-walk frequency noise); linear frequency drift produces $\sigma_y(\tau) \propto \tau$ and requires the Hadamard variance for drift-immune estimation.

\\sigma_y^2(\\tau).name: Two-Sample Allan Variance
\\sigma_y^2(\\tau).description: Dimensionless mean-squared fractional frequency instability at averaging interval $\tau$.

\\tau.name: Averaging Gate Time
\\tau.description: Duration of each contiguous non-overlapping measurement interval.

\\bar{y}_k.name: k-th Fractional Frequency Average
\\bar{y}_k.description: Time-averaged dimensionless fractional frequency offset $\Delta\nu/\nu_0$ over the $k$-th interval of length $\tau$.

\\bar{y}_{k+1}.name: (k+1)-th Fractional Frequency Average
\\bar{y}_{k+1}.description: Time-averaged dimensionless fractional frequency offset over the immediately following interval.

formulas.title: Bethe-Bloch Collisional Stopping Power
formulas.description: Gives the mean collisional energy loss per unit mass thickness $-\left\langle \frac{dE}{dx} \right\rangle$ for a moderately relativistic heavy charged particle of charge $ze$ and speed $\beta c$ ionizing a medium of atomic number $Z$, atomic mass $A$, and mean excitation energy $I$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: The Bethe-Bloch formula quantifies how charged particles slower than radiative thresholds decelerate via inelastic Coulomb scattering off bound atomic electrons.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A fast charged particle drags on atomic electrons as it passes through matter; slower particles linger longer and lose much more energy per centimeter, while relativistic particles settle into a nearly constant minimum-ionizing rate.
formulas.interpretation: The leading $1/\beta^2$ factor creates the sharp Bragg peak near the end of a particle's range, whereas the logarithmic factor produces a shallow minimum near $\beta\gamma \approx 3$ followed by a slow relativistic rise eventually tamed by dielectric density-effect screening.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Derived from first-order Born-approximation Coulomb scattering and the Thomas-Reiche-Kuhn dipole oscillator sum rule for bound atomic electrons.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Accurate to within a few percent for heavy charged particles ($M \gg m_e$) over $0.1 \lesssim \beta\gamma \lesssim 1000$; electrons require Mott exchange corrections and radiative bremsstrahlung terms, while ultra-high $\beta\gamma$ requires Fermi density-effect corrections.

\\left\\langle \\frac{dE}{dx} \\right\\r.name: Mean Mass Stopping Power
\\left\\langle \\frac{dE}{dx} \\right\\r.description: Average energy lost by the incident charged particle per unit mass thickness traversed.

K.name: Bethe-Bloch Constant
K.description: Universal stopping-power constant $4\pi N_A r_e^2 m_e c^2 \approx 0.307075\,\mathrm{MeV\,cm^2/mol}$.

z.name: Projectile Charge Number
z.description: Electric charge of the incident particle in units of the elementary charge $e$.

Z.name: Absorber Atomic Number
Z.description: Number of protons (and bound electrons) per atom of the absorbing medium.

A.name: Absorber Atomic Mass
A.description: Molar mass of the absorbing medium.

\\beta.name: Relativistic Velocity Ratio
\\beta.description: Ratio $v/c$ of the projectile speed to the vacuum speed of light.

m_e.name: Electron Rest Mass
m_e.description: Rest mass of the struck atomic electron ($m_e c^2 \approx 0.511\,\mathrm{MeV}$).

T_{\\max}.name: Maximum Single-Collision Energy Transfer
T_{\\max}.description: Largest kinetic energy that can be imparted to a free electron in a single head-on collision.

I.name: Mean Excitation Potential
I.description: Logarithmic average ionization and excitation energy of the absorber atoms.

formulas.title: Bremsstrahlung Exponential Radiation-Length Attenuation
formulas.description: Describes the exponential decay of mean electron energy $E(x)$ with absorber depth $x$ due to high-energy bremsstrahlung radiation, characterized by the material radiation length $X_0$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Defines the radiation length $X_0$ as the characteristic distance over which a high-energy electron loses all but $1/e$ of its initial energy $E_0$ to radiative photon emission.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A high-energy electron deflected by heavy atomic nuclei radiates away a fixed fraction of its remaining energy per radiation length, causing its energy to drop exponentially.
formulas.interpretation: Because radiative energy loss scales linearly with $E$ in the complete-screening regime ($-dE/dx = E/X_0$), high-energy electrons lose energy far faster than heavy muons or protons, whose bremsstrahlung rate is suppressed by $m^{-2}$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from integrating the scale-invariant Bethe-Heitler complete-screening differential bremsstrahlung cross-section over photon energies.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid for ultra-relativistic electrons and positrons well above the critical energy ($E \gg E_c$) where radiative losses dominate over Bethe-Bloch ionization and before Landau-Pomeranchuk-Migdal suppression sets in at multi-TeV energies.

E(x).name: Mean Electron Energy at Depth x
E(x).description: Expected remaining energy of the primary electron after traversing thickness $x$.

E_0.name: Incident Electron Energy
E_0.description: Initial kinetic plus rest energy of the electron entering the absorber at $x = 0$.

x.name: Absorber Depth
x.description: Mass thickness (or linear length) of material traversed by the electron.

X_0.name: Radiation Length
X_0.description: Material-dependent characteristic length scaling approximately as $A / (Z^2 \ln(183 Z^{-1/3}))$.

formulas.title: Electromagnetic Cascade Shower Maximum Depth
formulas.description: Gives the longitudinal depth $t_{\max} = x_{\max}/X_0$ in radiation lengths where an electromagnetic cascade initiated by energy $E_0$ reaches maximum particle multiplicity before ionization below critical energy $E_c$ terminates multiplication.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Predicts the peak depth of an electromagnetic shower inside a calorimeter as a logarithmic function of incident energy.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Because each shower generation roughly doubles the number of electrons and photons and halves their energy per radiation length, reaching the stopping threshold takes a number of steps proportional to $\ln(E_0/E_c)$.
formulas.interpretation: The logarithmic growth of $t_{\max}$ with $E_0$ explains why electromagnetic calorimeters can contain multi-TeV electrons within only 20 to 25 radiation lengths without growing proportionally in physical size.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Derived from the Heitler binary branching cascade model and refined by Rossi-Greisen Mellin-transform shower transport equations.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Applies to pure electromagnetic showers with $E_0 \gg E_c$; the offset $C_0 = -0.5$ for incident electrons and $C_0 = +0.5$ for incident photons due to the initial pair-production conversion depth.

t_{\\max}.name: Shower Maximum Depth
t_{\\max}.description: Longitudinal depth $x_{\max}/X_0$ of peak energy deposition in dimensionless units of radiation length.

E_0.name: Incident Shower Energy
E_0.description: Initial energy of the primary electron or photon entering the calorimeter.

E_c.name: Critical Energy
E_c.description: Threshold energy at which an electron's collisional ionization rate equals its radiative bremsstrahlung rate.

C_0.name: Primary-Species Depth Offset
C_0.description: Dimensionless offset equal to $-0.5$ for incident electrons and $+0.5$ for incident photons.

formulas.title: Cherenkov Coherent Emission Angle
formulas.description: Determines the polar emission angle $\theta_C$ of coherent Cherenkov light radiated by a charged particle moving at speed $\beta c$ through a transparent dielectric of refractive index $n$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Relates the opening angle of the optical Mach cone emitted by a superluminal charge in a dielectric directly to its relativistic velocity $\beta$.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Just as a supersonic jet creates a V-shaped acoustic shock cone, a charge outrunning light inside glass or water trails a glowing cone whose angle directly measures the particle's speed.
formulas.interpretation: Real emission angles exist strictly above the threshold $\beta > 1/n$; measuring $\theta_C$ in ring-imaging Cherenkov detectors provides high-precision particle identification when paired with magnetic momentum measurements.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from Huygens wavefront phase-matching and cylindrical translation invariance along a uniform rectilinear charge trajectory in a dispersive linear dielectric.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid for $\beta n > 1$ in a non-absorbing, locally isotropic dielectric over optical wavelengths where $n(\omega) > 1$; finite track length introduces diffraction broadening of the ring angle.

\\theta_C.name: Cherenkov Emission Angle
\\theta_C.description: Polar angle between the particle velocity vector and the emitted photon wavevector.

\\beta.name: Relativistic Velocity Ratio
\\beta.description: Ratio $v/c$ of the charged particle's speed to the vacuum speed of light.

n.name: Medium Refractive Index
n.description: Phase refractive index of the dielectric radiator at the detected optical frequency.

formulas.title: Highland Multiple Coulomb Scattering Width
formulas.description: Approximates the root-mean-square width $\theta_0$ of the central Gaussian core of the projected planar angular distribution after a particle of charge $ze$, speed $\beta c$, and momentum $p$ undergoes multiple small-angle Coulomb scatterings across thickness $x/X_0$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Quantifies the random-walk angular deflection accumulated by a charged track passing through detector material.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Thousands of tiny nudges from atomic nuclei jitter a track's direction like a random walk, spreading the angle proportional to the square root of material thickness and inversely proportional to momentum.
formulas.interpretation: Because $\theta_0$ scales inversely with $\beta c p$, multiple scattering dominates tracking uncertainty for low-momentum particles and sets a strict material-budget ceiling for vertex detectors.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Arises from central-limit Gaussian approximation to Moliere's small-angle azimuthally symmetric Coulomb transport distribution.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Accurate to roughly 11 percent over $10^{-3} < x/X_0 < 100$ (with a logarithmic $[1 + 0.038\ln(x/X_0)]$ refinement for precision fits); excludes the non-Gaussian single-scattering Rutherford tails beyond $3\theta_0$.

\\theta_0.name: Projected RMS Scattering Angle
\\theta_0.description: Standard deviation of the Gaussian core of the projected deflection angle in a single plane.

\\beta.name: Relativistic Velocity Ratio
\\beta.description: Ratio $v/c$ of the particle speed to the vacuum speed of light.

c.name: Speed of Light
c.description: Vacuum speed of light converting momentum $p$ to energy units $cp$.

p.name: Particle Momentum
p.description: Magnitude of the relativistic three-momentum of the traversing particle.

z.name: Projectile Charge Number
z.description: Charge of the incident particle in units of the elementary charge $e$.

x.name: Traversed Material Thickness
x.description: Path length of the particle through the scattering medium.

X_0.name: Radiation Length
X_0.description: Radiation length of the scattering medium in matching length or mass-thickness units.

formulas.title: Magnetic Spectrometer Tracking Sagitta
formulas.description: Relates the midpoint arc deviation (sagitta) $s$ of a singly charged particle track in a uniform transverse magnetic field $B$ over lever arm $L$ to its transverse momentum $p_T$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Converts the measurable geometric curvature of a charged trajectory inside a magnetic spectrometer directly into transverse momentum.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A stronger magnet or longer tracking arm bends a charged particle's path further from a straight line, while stiffer high-momentum tracks bend less and yield a smaller sagitta.
formulas.interpretation: Because $s \propto B L^2 / p_T$, fractional momentum uncertainty $\sigma_{p_T}/p_T = \sigma_s/s$ grows linearly with $p_T$, motivating multi-tesla superconducting magnets and large detector radii at high-energy colliders.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from circular cyclotron motion under the magnetic Lorentz force ($p_T = 0.3\,B R$) combined with the small-angle chord-sagitta theorem $s \approx L^2/(8R)$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid for singly charged particles ($|z|=1$) in a uniform field $B$ (in tesla) over projected path length $L$ (in meters) with $p_T$ in GeV/$c$, assuming small bending angles ($L \ll 2R$).

s.name: Track Sagitta
s.description: Maximum perpendicular distance between the curved circular trajectory and the straight chord connecting its endpoints.

B.name: Magnetic Field Strength
B.description: Uniform magnetic flux density perpendicular to the bending plane.

L.name: Spectrometer Lever Arm
L.description: Projected chord length of the measured track segment inside the magnetic field.

p_T.name: Transverse Momentum
p_T.description: Component of the particle's relativistic momentum perpendicular to the magnetic field axis.

formulas.title: Sampling Calorimeter Fractional Energy Resolution
formulas.description: Parameterizes the relative energy resolution $\sigma_E/E$ of an electromagnetic or hadronic calorimeter as the quadrature sum ($\oplus$) of a stochastic sampling term $a/\sqrt{E}$, an electronic noise term $b/E$, and a systematic constant floor $c$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Decomposes calorimeter measurement precision into three physically distinct statistical and instrumental error regimes across energy.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Calorimeters become fractionally more accurate at higher energies because larger showers contain more statistically independent tracks, until electronic noise fades and calibration imperfections set a hard floor.
formulas.interpretation: Unlike magnetic spectrometers whose fractional resolution degrades linearly with momentum, calorimeter precision improves as $E^{-1/2}$ across intermediate energies before saturating at the constant term $c$, making calorimetry indispensable at multi-hundred-GeV scales.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from error propagation of statistically independent Gaussian variance components: Poisson shower track counting ($N \propto E$), energy-independent readout noise, and multiplicative calibration nonuniformities.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Standard parameterization for well-contained showers with $E$ expressed in GeV; $a$ carries units of $\mathrm{GeV}^{1/2}$, $b$ carries units of $\mathrm{GeV}$, and $c$ is dimensionless.

\\sigma_E.name: Energy Measurement Standard Deviation
\\sigma_E.description: Root-mean-square uncertainty of the reconstructed shower energy.

E.name: Incident Particle Energy
E.description: Total energy deposited by the primary particle in the calorimeter.

a.name: Stochastic Resolution Coefficient
a.description: Coefficient governing Poisson sampling and photostatistics fluctuations scaling as $E^{-1/2}$.

b.name: Electronic Noise Coefficient
b.description: Energy-equivalent root-mean-square electronic readout noise and pileup contribution.

c.name: Constant Resolution Floor
c.description: Dimensionless systematic floor from channel inter-calibration, mechanical nonuniformity, and longitudinal shower leakage.

formulas.title: Helium-3/Helium-4 Dilution Refrigerator Cooling Power
formulas.description: Quantifies the steady-state cooling power $\dot{Q}$ (in watts) of a continuous $^3\mathrm{He}/^4\mathrm{He}$ dilution refrigerator mixing chamber at temperature $T_m$ (in kelvin) for a molar $^3\mathrm{He}$ circulation rate $\dot{n}_3$ (in $\mathrm{mol\,s^{-1}}$), arising from the molar enthalpy difference $H_d(T_m) - H_c(T_m) \approx 84\,T_m^2\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ across the phase boundary.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Gives the fundamental thermodynamic cooling capacity of a dilution refrigerator driven by transferring fermionic $^3\mathrm{He}$ atoms from the concentrated phase into the dilute superfluid $^4\mathrm{He}$-rich phase.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Pumping helium-3 atoms from a concentrated liquid into a dilute superfluid helium-4 mixture acts like evaporation that never runs out of vapor pressure, absorbing heat proportional to flow rate and the square of temperature.
formulas.interpretation: Because the dilute phase retains a finite $6.6\%$ solubility of $^3\mathrm{He}$ even as $T_m \to 0$, cooling power decreases only algebraically as $T_m^2$ rather than exponentially like evaporative cryostats, enabling continuous operation down to a few millikelvin.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from the low-temperature Sommerfeld expansion of two degenerate Fermi liquids with distinct Fermi temperatures ($T_{F,c} > T_{F,d}$) in osmotic equilibrium inside a Bose-condensed $^4\mathrm{He}$ superfluid background.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid in the degenerate Fermi-liquid regime ($T_m \lesssim 40\,\mathrm{mK}$) assuming ideal counterflow heat exchange so incoming concentrated $^3\mathrm{He}$ enters the mixing chamber at $T_m$; viscous heating and Kapitza resistance limit the achievable minimum temperature.

\\dot{Q}.name: Mixing Chamber Cooling Power
\\dot{Q}.description: Rate of thermal energy absorbed at the mixing chamber stage.

\\dot{n}_3.name: Helium-3 Molar Circulation Rate
\\dot{n}_3.description: Molar flux of $^3\mathrm{He}$ atoms crossing from the concentrated phase into the dilute phase.

T_m.name: Mixing Chamber Temperature
T_m.description: Absolute thermodynamic temperature of the $^3\mathrm{He}/^4\mathrm{He}$ phase boundary inside the mixing chamber.

formulas.title: Adiabatic Demagnetization Isentropic Temperature Scaling
formulas.description: Determines the final temperature $T_f$ achieved by isentropically demagnetizing a paramagnetic or nuclear spin system from initial temperature $T_i$ and applied magnetic field $B_i$ to final field $B_f$ in the presence of an effective internal dipolar and exchange field $b$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Expresses entropy conservation of a weakly interacting spin ensemble whose thermodynamic entropy depends solely on the ratio of total effective magnetic field $\sqrt{B^2 + b^2}$ to absolute temperature $T$.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Reducing the external magnetic field on thermally isolated spins forces their temperature to drop in lockstep so spin disorder stays constant, bottoming out only when the tiny internal magnetic field between neighboring spins takes over.
formulas.interpretation: In the ideal limit $B_f \gg b$, temperature scales linearly as $T_f = T_i (B_f / B_i)$; as $B_f \to 0$, the internal local field $b$ prevents reaching absolute zero and sets the minimum base temperature $T_{\min} = T_i b / \sqrt{B_i^2 + b^2}$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Derived from the dimensionless scaling argument $\mu B_{\mathrm{eff}} / (k_B T)$ of the Brillouin paramagnetic partition function along an adiabatic isentrope ($dS = 0$).
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Applies to reversible, thermally isolated demagnetization where lattice heat capacity is negligible compared to spin heat capacity and eddy-current heating is suppressed; breaks down below the spontaneous spin-ordering temperature.

T_f.name: Final Spin Temperature
T_f.description: Absolute temperature reached after adiabatic field reduction.

T_i.name: Initial Precooling Temperature
T_i.description: Starting temperature of the magnetized spin stage before thermal isolation.

B_f.name: Final Applied Magnetic Field
B_f.description: External magnetic flux density remaining at the end of demagnetization.

B_i.name: Initial Applied Magnetic Field
B_i.description: Initial external magnetizing flux density applied during isothermal heat rejection.

b.name: Effective Internal Local Field
b.description: Root-mean-square intrinsic dipolar and exchange magnetic field generated by neighboring spins.

formulas.title: Kapitza Acoustic Interfacial Thermal Resistance
formulas.description: Defines the Kapitza interfacial thermal resistance $R_K$ as the ratio of the discontinuous temperature jump $\Delta T$ across a solid-liquid or solid-solid boundary to the areal heat flux $\dot{Q}/A$, scaling inversely with the cube of absolute temperature $T^{-3}$ in the acoustic mismatch model.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Measures the thermal impedance caused by strong reflection of acoustic phonons at an interface between two media with mismatched mass densities and sound speeds.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Heat crossing from a cold metal into liquid helium hits an acoustic bottleneck because sound waves mostly bounce off the boundary, creating a sharp temperature step that worsens dramatically as temperature drops.
formulas.interpretation: Because the phonon specific heat scales as $T^3$ at low temperatures, the interfacial thermal conductance $G_K = R_K^{-1}$ vanishes as $T^3$, forcing sub-kelvin heat exchangers to use porous sintered metal powders with huge surface area $A$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from Snell's law acoustic transmission coefficients integrated over three-dimensional Debye phonon phase space obeying Planck-Bose occupation statistics.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid in the small temperature-drop linear-response regime ($\Delta T \ll T$) well below the Debye temperature; surface roughness, adsorbed helium layers, and magnetic coupling can enhance conductance beyond pure acoustic mismatch predictions.

R_K.name: Kapitza Thermal Boundary Resistance
R_K.description: Areal thermal impedance across the material interface.

\\Delta T.name: Interfacial Temperature Jump
\\Delta T.description: Discontinuous temperature difference across the boundary under steady heat flow.

\\dot{Q}.name: Interfacial Heat Current
\\dot{Q}.description: Total thermal power transmitted across the boundary.

A.name: Effective Interfacial Area
A.description: Microscopic contact surface area separating the two thermal media.

T.name: Mean Interface Temperature
T.description: Absolute thermodynamic temperature of the boundary region.

formulas.title: Tersoff-Hamann Differential Tunneling Conductance
formulas.description: Relates the voltage derivative of the scanning tunneling current $\frac{dI}{dV}(V)$ at bias voltage $V$ directly to the sample's local electronic density of states $\rho_s(\mathbf{r}_0, E_F + eV)$ evaluated at the tip apex center $\mathbf{r}_0$ and energy $E_F + eV$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Establishes scanning tunneling spectroscopy as a direct real-space and energy-resolved probe of surface electronic wavefunctions and quasiparticle spectral weight.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Sweeping the bias voltage on a sharp metallic tip reveals how many electronic states exist at each energy right underneath the tip, turning electrical conductance into a local quantum map.
formulas.interpretation: In the zero-temperature limit, the Fermi-Dirac derivative becomes a Dirac delta function so $\frac{dI}{dV}$ isolates states at energy $E_F + eV$; at finite temperature $T$, spectral features are convolved with a thermal broadening kernel of width $\approx 3.5\,k_B T$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Derived from Bardeen's time-dependent tunneling matrix element assuming a rotationally invariant $s$-wave tip wavefunction with energy-independent tip density of states.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid in the weak-tunneling regime where tip and sample wavefunctions overlap perturbatively and bias voltage $|eV|$ remains small compared to the vacuum work function $\phi$; $p$-wave or $d$-wave tip orbitals introduce lateral derivative weights.

\\frac{dI}{dV}.name: Differential Tunneling Conductance
\\frac{dI}{dV}.description: Derivative of tunneling current $I$ with respect to tip-sample bias voltage $V$.

V.name: Tip-Sample Bias Voltage
V.description: Applied electrostatic potential difference shifting the sample Fermi level relative to the tip.

\\rho_s.name: Sample Local Density of States
\\rho_s.description: Probability density of sample electronic eigenstates per unit energy at tip apex position $\mathbf{r}_0$.

\\mathbf{r}_0.name: Tip Apex Center Position
\\mathbf{r}_0.description: Three-dimensional coordinate of the center of curvature of the scanning tip apex.

E_F.name: Fermi Energy
E_F.description: Equilibrium chemical potential of the conducting sample.

e.name: Elementary Charge
e.description: Magnitude of the electric charge carried by a single electron.

formulas.title: Vacuum Tunneling Inverse Decay Length
formulas.description: Gives the exponential spatial decay constant $\kappa$ of an electron wavefunction penetrating a classically forbidden vacuum barrier of effective work function $\phi$ for an electron of mass $m_e$ with reduced Planck constant $\hbar$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Sets the characteristic sub-angstrom length scale governing the exponential attenuation of tunneling probability $T(z) \propto e^{-2\kappa z}$ across a vacuum gap.
formulas.intuitive_summary: A higher work function barrier makes the electron wavefunction die off faster in empty space, which is why moving an STM tip by a single atom width changes the tunneling current by a factor of ten.
formulas.interpretation: For a typical metallic work function $\phi \approx 4\,\mathrm{eV}$, $\kappa \approx 1.0\,\text{\AA}^{-1}$, so $2\kappa \approx 2.0\,\text{\AA}^{-1}$ and the current drops by roughly $e^2 \approx 7.4$ per angstrom of retraction, concentrating current almost entirely through the foremost apex atom.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows directly from the imaginary wavevector solution $k = i\kappa$ of the one-dimensional time-independent Schrödinger equation in a constant potential region $U_0 - E = \phi$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid for low bias ($|eV| \ll \phi$) and negligible lateral surface wavevector ($k_\parallel = 0$); states with nonzero parallel momentum decay more rapidly as $\sqrt{\kappa^2 + k_\parallel^2}$, and image-charge rounding slightly lowers the effective barrier.

\\kappa.name: Vacuum Tunneling Inverse Decay Length
\\kappa.description: Exponential attenuation rate of the evanescent electron wavefunction inside the vacuum gap.

m_e.name: Electron Rest Mass
m_e.description: Inertial mass of an electron tunneling through vacuum.

\\phi.name: Effective Vacuum Barrier Height
\\phi.description: Average work function energy separating the Fermi level from the vacuum level.

formulas.title: Frequency-Modulated AFM Cantilever Resonance Shift
formulas.description: Approximates the resonance frequency shift $\Delta f$ of a frequency-modulated atomic force microscope cantilever of unperturbed eigenfrequency $f_0$ and flexural spring constant $k_c$ subjected to a small vertical tip-sample force gradient $\frac{\partial F_{ts}}{\partial z}$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Converts microscopic interatomic force gradients into a high-precision frequency measurement by linearizing the effective harmonic stiffness $k_{\mathrm{eff}} = k_c - \partial F_{ts}/\partial z$.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Attractive surface forces soften the cantilever spring and lower its oscillation frequency, whereas repulsive atomic forces stiffen it and push the pitch upward.
formulas.interpretation: Because phase-locked loops measure frequency shifts to millihertz precision even in high-Q vacuum cantilevers, $\Delta f$ enables non-contact atomic resolution on insulators without snapping the tip into contact.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows from first-order Taylor expansion of the harmonic oscillator eigenfrequency $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{(k_c + k_{ts})/m_{\mathrm{eff}}}$ for $|k_{ts}| \ll k_c$.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Strict small-amplitude limit where oscillation amplitude $A$ is much smaller than the decay length of $F_{ts}(z)$; for larger amplitudes, $\Delta f$ becomes a weighted integral over the oscillation cycle via the Sader-Jarvis deconvolution formula.

\\Delta f.name: Cantilever Resonance Frequency Shift
\\Delta f.description: Change in fundamental oscillation frequency induced by tip-sample interaction forces.

f_0.name: Unperturbed Cantilever Eigenfrequency
f_0.description: Free-space fundamental flexural resonance frequency far from the sample.

k_c.name: Cantilever Flexural Spring Constant
k_c.description: Elastic restoring stiffness of the cantilever tip in the vertical direction.

\\frac{\\partial F_{ts}}{\\partial z}.name: Vertical Tip-Sample Force Gradient
\\frac{\\partial F_{ts}}{\\partial z}.description: Spatial derivative of the normal tip-sample interaction force $F_{ts}$ with respect to tip height $z$.

formulas.title: AFM Cantilever Equipartition Thermal Noise
formulas.description: Gives the equilibrium mean-squared vertical thermal displacement $\langle z_{\mathrm{th}}^2 \rangle$ of an atomic force microscope cantilever with spring constant $k_c$ in thermal equilibrium with a heat bath at temperature $T$, with Boltzmann constant $k_B$.
formulas.conceptual_definition: Establishes the fundamental classical Brownian deflection noise floor of a harmonic force sensor and provides a standard calibration route for cantilever stiffness.
formulas.intuitive_summary: Thermal energy constantly jiggles a microscopic cantilever like a tiny spring in a warm bath; stiffer springs and colder temperatures both shrink this unavoidable quiver.
formulas.interpretation: Integrating the thermal Lorentzian power spectral density over all frequencies yields $k_B T / k_c$ independent of damping or quality factor $Q$, while cooling from $300\,\mathrm{K}$ to $30\,\mathrm{mK}$ reduces root-mean-square deflection noise by a factor of $100$.
formulas.symmetry_origin: Follows directly from the classical equipartition theorem equating average quadratic elastic potential energy $\frac{1}{2} k_c \langle z_{\mathrm{th}}^2 \rangle$ to $\frac{1}{2} k_B T$ per harmonic degree of freedom.
formulas.limits_and_boundary: Valid in the classical thermal regime ($k_B T \gg \hbar \omega_0$) for the fundamental flexural mode; at ultralow temperatures where $k_B T \lesssim \hbar \omega_0$, zero-point quantum fluctuations $\hbar / (2 m_{\mathrm{eff}} \omega_0)$ supersede the classical floor.

\\langle z_{\\mathrm{th}}^2 \\rangle.name: Mean-Squared Thermal Deflection
\\langle z_{\\mathrm{th}}^2 \\rangle.description: Ensemble variance of the cantilever tip's vertical Brownian displacement.

k_B.name: Boltzmann Constant
k_B.description: Proportionality constant relating absolute temperature to thermal energy.

T.name: Absolute Bath Temperature
T.description: Thermodynamic temperature of the cantilever and its surrounding thermal reservoir.

k_c.name: Cantilever Flexural Spring Constant
k_c.description: Elastic restoring stiffness governing vertical cantilever deflection.
